newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Access sees faster Australia economy in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Access sees faster Australia economy in 97/98.

text.p: Consultancy Access Economics on Wednesday forecast the Australian economy would be substantially weaker in the fiscal year to June than the government projects.
But Access expected the economy, which has been in a flat spot for more than a year, to pick up in 1997/98.
Access said 1996/97 growth in gross domestic product, employment and consumer prices would be well below the forecasts than the government issued in August.

"We continue to expect only slow growth until mid-1997," Access said. "This is consistent with current employment and ANZ (Bank) job ads data, weak retail spending and the profit squeeze on industrial firms."
GDP would grow only 3.0 percent in 1996/97 from the previous year's level, compared with the government's forecast for such year-average growth of 3.5 percent, the consultancy said.
Underlying consumer prices, which exclude large volatile items, would be a year-average 2.3 percent higher than in 1995/96, Access said. The government projected 2.75 percent year-average inflation.

And since employment would grow 1.0 percent year-average in 1996/97, rather than the officially forecast 2.0 percent, Access said the unemployment rate would be 8.8 percent in the June quarter, not 8.25 percent.
The government is expected to revise its forecasts sometime this month.
However, Access's view of 1997/98 is significantly stronger than the government's, with a projection for GDP growth of 4.1 percent.

The government estimated 3.25 percent 1997/98 GDP growth in August, although Treasury says its more distant forecasts are relatively unreliable. It makes them only because it must have them for fiscal forecasts.
Australia's long-term trend GDP growth rate is a little over three percent per year.
Access's 1997/98 employment forecast, 2.1 percent, was similar to the government's 2.0 percent.
But despite its stronger view of 1997/98 activity, the consultancy was more optimistic on wages growth, currently a central determinant of monetary policy.
Average wages for 1996/97 would be 4.4 percent higher than a year before and and 3.5 percent higher the following year.
The government is forecasting wage growth of 5.0 percent and 4.5 percent in those years.
